All ancient structures—pyramids, hilltop castles, and even the Borobudur temple—originated from natural rock formations already present at those very sites. This ensured that the raw stone or limestone was already positioned exactly where it would be incorporated into the structure.
Based on my observations, a pyramid was originally a large, natural rock formation that was broken apart and reassembled on the exterior. The construction began at the peak’s corners and proceeded downward and outward, following a planned scale and design. Once the pyramid was assembled, its final height was significantly lower and shorter than the original rock formation; there was no need to haul stones upward. After the inner core of the natural rock was encased in layers of stone masonry, the interior was then carved out to create chambers and passageways. The complexity of these internal spaces and conduits exists precisely because they follow the natural structural veins and grain of the stone.
This is evidenced by the Sphinx, which was carved directly from a natural rock formation rather than being constructed from individual stone blocks like the pyramids. Further proof lies in the surrounding expanse of sand, which consists of debris—the remnants of stone carved away during the construction process.
